_doc.purpose: Physical facts about NAMED historical deposits, for sim/world/deposits.py's Ricardian rent mechanism. Nothing here is a price and nothing here is a quantity demanded - see that module's docstring for why demand is a caller-supplied parameter, never a constant. Each entry states three things a real ore body actually has: how rich it is (ore_grade_kg_per_tonne - kilograms of CONTAINED METAL per tonne of rock or gravel raised, not a fraction of the metal's own price), how it must be worked (depth_class, hardness_class - what raises or lowers the labour to break and haul that tonne), and, for the two metals geography.json does not carry a regional breakdown for (gold, mercury), its own explicit share_of_empire_output. For every other metal (iron, copper, tin, lead, silver) the QUANTITY a deposit can supply is deliberately NOT stated here: sim/world/deposits.py computes it from data/world/geography.json's own per-region mineral share times data/world/resources.json's empire_output_100ad, which is already-committed data this file has no business duplicating.
_doc.why_not_one_deposit_per_material: Every region in the Roman world (or, for gold and mercury, every region named in resources.json's own notes) that geography.json credits with a nonzero share of a metal gets its own entry, because that share IS an already-established fact about how much of the empire's output came from where - collapsing it to one national-average deposit per metal would throw away exactly the geographic variation (Elba's rich surface hematite against a generic Levantine iron placeholder; Las Medulas's alluvial gold against Dacia's hard vein gold) the task this file answers to asked for.
_doc.grade_is_never_a_price: ore_grade_kg_per_tonne is a geological fact - ore mineralogy, not a market observation - and sim/world/deposits.py's own tests check that nothing in this file or that module imports data/prices.json. Where a specific ancient assay is not available (most entries), the grade is a textbook order-of-magnitude figure for that ore type, marked confidence C or D and said so in `source`; it is never backed into matching a book price.
_doc.material_moved: 'ore' for rock broken out of a vein or bed; 'gravel' for loose alluvial material moved by panning or hydraulic sluicing rather than broken. The distinction matters because gravel needs no breaking labour at all - see depth_class 'alluvial' and 'alluvial_hydraulic' in sim/world/deposits.py.
_doc.region_field: Keys into data/world/geography.json's regions for every metal that file carries a mineral share for. Dacia is the one exception: resources.json's own gold note names it directly ('Las Medulas and, from 106 AD, Dacia') but geography.json has no Balkan/Dacian region, so that entry's region is the free-text label 'dacia' and is not looked up there - its quantity comes entirely from its own share_of_empire_output.
_doc.conf: Same A-D scale as data/prices.json and data/world/resources.json: B where a specific ancient source or an unusually well-documented deposit is named, C for a generic estimate of a known ore type, D for a placeholder standing in for a region this file's author could not find a specific ancient mine for.

iron.name: elba_hematite
iron.source: Elban hematite is repeatedly named among antiquity's richest and most heavily worked iron ores, mined from surface and near-surface outcrops on Elba since Etruscan times; 500 kg/t (50% Fe) is a round figure for rich, weathered hematite, not an assay of a specific Roman-era working.

iron.name: noricum_siderite
iron.source: Noricum (the eastern Alps) siderite/limonite ore, the basis of the famous 'Noricum steel' (ferrum Noricum) ancient sources repeatedly praise; 350 kg/t (35% Fe) is a round figure for siderite ore, below its theoretical maximum because real ore always carries gangue.

iron.name: wealden_bog_iron
iron.source: Wealden clay ironstone and lowland bog iron gathered near the surface rather than mined from a vein - lower grade than Elba's hematite, but requiring far less labour to break out, which is the whole reason bog iron was worth working at all before anyone owned a shaft.

iron.name: hispania_hematite
iron.source: Hematite associated with the oxidised cap of the Iberian Pyrite Belt, the same metallogenic province as the region's copper, lead and silver below; 400 kg/t is a round figure for good-quality hematite, not an assay.

iron.name: north_africa_iron_generic
iron.source: No specific ancient North African iron mine identified by this file's author; a generic mid-range ore-grade placeholder standing in for geography.json's 0.1 regional share so the region is not silently dropped from the supply curve.

iron.name: anatolian_iron
iron.source: Anatolia is the traditional heartland of early iron metallurgy (Hittite ironworking predates Rome by over a thousand years), so a working iron-ore tradition there by the Roman period is well attested even without a single named mine; 350 kg/t is a round mid-range figure.

iron.name: levant_iron_generic
iron.source: No specific ancient Levantine/Mesopotamian iron mine identified; generic placeholder for geography.json's 0.05 regional share, same reasoning as north_africa_iron_generic.

copper.name: italia_copper_generic
copper.source: Minor Etruscan-era copper working in Tuscany/Campania is attested but not at Rio Tinto's scale; generic 3% ore-grade placeholder for geography.json's small 0.02 share.

copper.name: gaul_germania_copper_generic
copper.source: Generic placeholder; pre-Roman Alpine/Rhineland copper working existed but no single dominant ancient mine identified by this file's author.

copper.name: britannia_copper_generic
copper.source: Generic placeholder for geography.json's 0.05 British copper share.

copper.name: rio_tinto_copper
copper.source: The Rio Tinto/Iberian Pyrite Belt massive sulfide deposit, one of the largest on Earth, worked to real depth in antiquity - the extensive underground galleries and the drainage-wheel batteries recovered from Roman-era workings there are the standard textbook example of ancient deep hard-rock mining requiring continuous dewatering. 60 kg/t (6% Cu) reflects the richer supergene-enriched zone ancient miners specifically targeted, not the deposit's much lower bulk average grade.

copper.name: anatolian_copper
copper.source: Anatolia has a copper-working tradition older than bronze itself (native and oxide copper worked since the Chalcolithic); 40 kg/t is a round mid-range figure for a worked oxide/carbonate ore, not an assay of one named mine.

copper.name: cyprus_copper
copper.source: Cyprus - the island the metal is named after - is worked in antiquity for its oxidised and carbonate copper ores (malachite, azurite, cuprite) in the weathered cap of its ore bodies, cherry-picked at or near the surface long before anyone dug for the much larger but far leaner sulfide ore beneath; 80 kg/t (8%) reflects that enriched cap, not the primary sulfide grade.

lead.name: italia_lead_generic
lead.source: Generic placeholder for geography.json's small 0.02 Italian lead share.

lead.name: gaul_germania_lead_generic
lead.source: Generic placeholder; pre-Roman central European galena working existed but no single dominant ancient mine identified.

lead.name: britannia_lead
lead.source: Mendip and Pennine galena veins, extensively worked from the earliest years of the Roman occupation (lead ingots (pigs) stamped with imperial ownership survive); 150 kg/t (15%) is a round figure for a good vein-galena ore.

lead.name: hispania_lead
lead.source: Cartagena/Sierra argentiferous galena, the same deep-worked district as rio_tinto_copper; 180 kg/t (18%) is a round figure for a rich galena vein.

lead.name: laurion_lead
lead.source: Laurion's galena, worked to genuine depth through hundreds of shafts over the Classical and Hellenistic periods; by the Roman era the readily accessible rich ore is long since taken and what remains is leaner and deeper, hence a lower grade than Britain's or Spain's fresher veins.

silver.name: italia_silver_generic
silver.source: Generic placeholder for geography.json's small 0.02 Italian silver share; silver is a trace constituent of argentiferous galena, not its own separate ore.

silver.name: britannia_silver_generic
silver.source: Silver content of British argentiferous lead ore (see britannia_lead); generic figure, no assay.

silver.name: hispania_silver
silver.source: Strabo, Geography 3.2.10, citing Polybius, on the silver mines near New Carthage: on the order of 40,000 workers and revenue to Rome of 25,000 drachmas a day - the single best-attested ancient claim of exceptional richness for any deposit in this file. 1.0 kg/t (0.1% Ag) is a correspondingly generous silver content for argentiferous galena, at the rich end of what such ore can carry.

silver.name: laurion_silver
silver.source: Laurion's silver-lead ore funded the Athenian navy centuries before Rome arrived (Xenophon, Ways and Means, describes the mines at length); by the Roman period the field is old and deep-shafted with its richest ore long extracted, hence a lower silver content than Hispania's fresher workings, not a claim it was ever poor.

tin.name: gaul_germania_tin_generic
tin.source: Generic placeholder for geography.json's small 0.1 share; alluvial cassiterite in Rhine-system gravels, no specific ancient working identified.

tin.name: cornish_tin_streaming
tin.source: Cornish and Devon 'streaming' of cassiterite (tin ore, dense enough to naturally concentrate in river gravel) is the classic ancient British tin industry, already well known to Mediterranean traders by Herodotus's time; worked with simple ground-sluicing and panning, not the aqueduct-fed hydraulic works Rome later builds for gold at Las Medulas.

tin.name: hispania_tin_generic
tin.source: Iberian alluvial cassiterite is attested (geography.json's own located_materials lists hispania among tin's regions) but without a single named ancient working; generic mid-range placer grade.

gold.name: las_medulas_alluvial
gold.source: Pliny, Natural History 33.66-78, describes the 'ruina montium' method at Las Medulas in detail: aqueducts brought water from many kilometres away to collapse whole hillsides and wash the resulting gravel through sluice channels, which is exactly why this entry's hardness_class is null and its depth_class is 'alluvial_hydraulic' rather than plain 'alluvial' - the labour of BREAKING the ground is done by water, not by hand. 0.0003 kg/t (0.3 g/t) is an order-of-magnitude placer-gold grade typical of a large hydraulic operation, not an assayed figure; share_of_empire_output is this file's own estimate, standing in for the regional breakdown geography.json does not carry for gold - see this file's _doc.

gold.name: dacia_vein_gold
gold.source: data/world/resources.json's own gold entry names Dacia, opened to Roman exploitation after the conquest of 106 AD, as a second source alongside Las Medulas; the Dacian gold-quartz veins (the Rosia Montana district) are hard-rock epithermal veins worked underground, not placer gravel. 0.008 kg/t (8 g/t) is a typical order-of-magnitude epithermal vein-gold grade, not a specific assay. Region is the free-text label 'dacia': geography.json has no Balkan/Dacian region to key into, so this entry's quantity comes entirely from share_of_empire_output, never from a geography.json lookup - see this file's _doc.

mercury.name: almaden_cinnabar
mercury.source: Almaden is repeatedly described in the historical-geology literature as among the richest cinnabar (mercury sulfide) deposits ever worked, with ore grades far above the low-single-digit-percent typical of most mercury deposits; 50 kg/t (5% Hg) is a round figure well within its historically reported range, not an assay of a specific Roman-period working. Roman-era exploitation is documented as a convict/damnati-ad-metalla operation under imperial monopoly (see data/world/geography.json's mercury note); depth_class is 'shallow_vein' for the Roman-era workings specifically - the deposit was later worked far deeper, over many further centuries, which is outside this era.

mercury.name: monte_amiata_cinnabar
mercury.source: Tuscan (Monte Amiata) cinnabar, worked since Etruscan times, markedly lower grade than Almaden's - this is Complaints/32's own 'about three cinnabar deposits worth working in the Roman world': Almaden and Monte Amiata are the two this file names, both genuinely workable, at very different grades.
